one_line_contribution: A dense factorial + oracle-baseline measurement claiming that the entire class of policies that decide a memory item's fate before the query is known is bounded near random selection at matched injection volume, while an untrained query-conditional reranker (C6) exceeds even an oracle static prune (C3) handed unlimited outcome supervision.
closest_prior_work: Two threats, in different directions. (1) arXiv:2603.02473 (retrieval-vs-utilization factorial on LoCoMo) already establishes the direction; the proposal concedes this and re-centres on the bound, the volume control, and the variance decomposition, which is the right move and largely works. (2) The more damaging one the proposal treats as settled: KATE (Liu et al., 2021) and Rubin et al. (2022) for query-conditional demonstration retrieval, plus the standard bi-encoder-retrieve/cross-encoder-rerank result from IR. The proposal's headline positive finding (F6: C6 beats C3, C1, C4, C9, C10) is, mechanically, 'a cross-encoder reranker over the top-12 beats a bi-encoder top-4 with 12 of 120 bank items deleted.' That is a known IR result wearing a memory-curation costume; the proposal's own Related Work concedes the direction is anticipated by KATE but then defends the magnitude and the no-supervision framing, neither of which survives if the operative variable is the relevance model rather than conditionality.
strongest_objection: P1 is not a ceiling on query-agnostic policies, and F1 is close to tautological. All 8 Phase-1 configurations are fixed rank patterns of size 4 drawn from *the retriever's own query-conditional top-12*. A 'constant' choice of rank pattern therefore inherits essentially all of the retriever's query-conditionality; the only thing held query-agnostic is which ranks among 12 already-topically-relevant candidates get used. Finding that no fixed rank pattern beats a random rank pattern by >2 points (F1) says the top-12 are roughly exchangeable in rank order — it says nothing about the audited class, which decides *item identity in the bank*, not rank position at read time. The paper's Risk Factor 3 acknowledges the pool restriction but frames it as a fairness issue ('a richer pool could raise the static ceiling somewhat'); the actual problem is a construct-validity failure, not a power one. Compounding it in Phase 3: C1/C2/C3/C9 all remove 12 items from a 120-item bank from which retrieval injects only 4. For most queries the deleted items were never in the top-4, so the F5 null band (all static conditions within ±3 of random removal) is close to mechanically guaranteed regardless of whether write-time curation carries real signal — and the plan never reports, or controls for, how often removed items would have entered the top-4. A reviewer will read the centrepiece as a bound on rank-pattern selection and the audit as a null manufactured by a 10% prune, and the abstract's claim that 'any published write-time curation gain exceeding the measured static ceiling must come from bank shrinkage' will not be supported by either.
what_would_fix_it: (1) Add a genuinely query-agnostic arm to Phase 1: a fixed *item-identity* set (the same 4 bank items injected for every query, best-of-pool fitted LOO). The gap between that and the best fixed rank pattern is the actual query-agnostic ceiling, and reporting both separates 'the retriever is doing the work' from 'staticness is bounded'. (2) Break the C6/C3 confound by adding a cross-encoder-matched static arm — e.g. a globally fixed item ordering scored by the same cross-encoder against a query-independent probe, and/or C3+cross-encoder-read as a crossed 2x2 of {static prune, no prune} x {bi-encoder read, cross-encoder read}. Without the crossing, F6 measures reranker quality, not policy class. (3) Sweep the prune fraction (e.g. 10/30/50% of the bank) rather than fixing it at 12/120, and report the rate at which removed items would have appeared in the deployment top-4; a null at a prune depth that barely perturbs retrieval is uninformative. (4) Make the Phase-0 precheck noise-controlled: '≥8% of instances differ in either direction' between memory and no-memory is within the 2.2-6.0 point agentic decoding variance the proposal itself cites, so the gate can pass on noise; require a seed-replicated, paired disagreement rate above the null-replicate band. (5) Either raise Phase-1 to give P2 real training data or drop F2's threshold: a configuration x query-feature interaction model over ~50 features and 8 configurations fitted on 199 instances, with an MDE of 4.4 against a predicted effect of 5, is a coin flip by construction and will most likely land in the pre-declared 'inconclusive' band or in Branch C.
missing_baseline: A query-agnostic arm that receives the same relevance-model upgrade as C6 — i.e. cross-encoder scoring applied query-independently (a globally fixed cross-encoder-ranked item list, or C3's oracle prune read with the cross-encoder). As written, C6 is the only arm in the paper with a cross-encoder in the read path, so every C6-vs-static comparison in F6 is 'cross-encoder vs BGE' rather than 'conditional vs query-agnostic'. Secondary omissions a reviewer will also demand: a fixed-item-set (same 4 items for all queries) arm in Phase 1, and a no-memory arm in Phase 3 — given this track's own prior finding that memory injection can be one-sidedly harmful, a Phase-3 table in which every curation condition sits within noise of no-memory would reinterpret the entire audit, and the Phase-0 precheck on 150 dev instances does not substitute for it.
preprint_collision: Well above average and I credit it: it names arXiv:2603.02473 as a partial collision, concedes the directional finding rather than burying it, states a decidable disagreement (C3 vs C2, P1 vs P0), and retracts a prior anchor citation (MEMAUDIT, arXiv:2605.02199) it could not re-verify. Three real gaps remain. First, it admits it could retrieve only title/venue for A-MAC (arXiv:2603.04549), yet the plan pre-registers a 'faithful A-MAC reimplementation' with a specific five-factor score (future utility, factual confidence, semantic novelty, recency, content-type prior) and makes C1-vs-C2 a headline comparison — you cannot pre-commit to fidelity against a paper whose abstract you could not read, and the fidelity check ('reproduce the direction of its published end-to-end effect') is unverifiable against an unretrieved result. Second, the search is entirely on the agent-memory side; there is no recency pass at all on the two literatures where a collision with the *positive* finding is most likely — query-conditional/instance-adaptive demonstration selection post-KATE, and cross-encoder reranking for memory/experience retrieval. Given that F6 is the boldest claim and is exactly a cross-encoder reranking result, the absence of any preprint search in that space is a substantive hole, not a formality. Third, the residual risk it names (a matched-volume random-removal ablation buried in a recent curation preprint's appendix) is real and unresolved, and that control is one of the three things it claims as remaining novelty.
